Acrylic paint-along · beginner

A black-capped chickadee perched on an autumn branch

Start on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

18 stepsCanvas: 14 x 11 inFocal point: the bird's head Light: the low sun, upper right: warm light on the right of the bird and branch, cool blue-gray shadow on the leftHow this lesson was made

Brushes

  • 1 inch flat: Cover the canvas with misty lavender-grayFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • 3/4 inch flat: Glow gold around the sunFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • #8 round: Dab in the sunRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • 1/2 inch old stiff flat: Dab the hazy orange foliageOld stiff flat: worn, splayed bristles, for rough texture like grass and foliage
  • 1/2 inch flat: Block in the round tan bodyFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • #6 round: Light the cream chestRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • 1/4 inch angle: Darken the wing feathersAngle: flat cut on a slant, for crisp corners and curves
  • #4 round: Press in the white cheekRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • 10/0 liner: Draw the legs and feetLiner: long, very thin bristles, for fine lines like twigs and grass

Also

  • A 14 x 11 in canvas, landscape (hang it that way), and masking tape to mark halves and quarters along its edges.
  • Water jar and paper towel
  • Palette or paper plate for mixing

Your paints

Every paint in the lesson. You don't have to mix them all at the start: each step lists the paints it uses with their recipes, so you can mix a little as you go before it dries. Parts are by volume.

Before you start

Mark halves and quarters on tape

Run a strip of masking tape along the top edge of the canvas and one down a side, and mark the middle and the quarters on each. On your 14 x 11 in canvas the marks across the top are 3 1/2 in apart and the marks down the side 2 3/4 in apart. Every step's Where picture has the same lines, so you can find its place on your canvas. (Chalk lines on the canvas would be painted over by the first coat; the tape stays.)

The transfer outline (optional)

The outlines of the main shapes, on the same quarter grid as your tape: 1 The four leaves; 2 The chickadee. Before the stage that starts one, you can lightly chalk its outline on the canvas, using the tape marks to place it.

Strokes to try on scrap paper first

Each one's card is open in the step that first uses it.

  • Side-to-side blend, first in step 1.
  • X stroke, first in step 2.
  • Small circles, first in step 3.
  • Dabbing, first in step 4.
  • Pull-down, first in step 5.
  • Curved strokes, first in step 8.
  • Dry brush, first in step 9. Try it on scrap paper first: wipe the brush until it leaves broken marks.
  • Press and lift, first in step 10. Try a row of them on scrap paper first.
  • Building from pieces, first in step 12.
  • Thick to thin, first in step 15.
  • Liner work, first in step 18. Try a few lines on scrap paper first.

The basics

Before you start not checked yet

Before you start

Not checked yet

  • Two water jars: one to rinse the brush, one kept clean for thinning paint. A big clear jar shows when the rinse water is dirty.
  • A rag or paper towel, to wipe the brush between colors.
  • Put out bigger puddles of paint than you think you need. Big puddles stay wet longer than small smears.
  • Lay your colors out the same way every time, so they're easy to find and don't get dragged into each other.
Keep your colors clean not checked yet

Keep your colors clean

Not checked yet

  • Wipe the brush on a rag between colors.
  • Rinse it fully before going into white.
  • Rinse often. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  • Mix on the palette, not on the canvas. Two or three colors at most: stop when the color is right.
Colors dry darker not checked yet

Colors dry darker

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic looks lighter when wet than when dry.
  • Before a big area, paint a test swatch and let it dry before judging the mix.
Fixing a mistake not checked yet

Fixing a mistake

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic is forgiving. Let the area dry, then paint over it and try again.
  • Don't keep working a spot that's half dry. Leave it, work somewhere else, and come back.
Keep paint from drying on the palette not checked yet

Keep paint from drying on the palette

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic on a brushstroke stays wet for only a few minutes.
  • Mist the palette lightly with a spray bottle now and then. Only lightly: too much water weakens the paint.
  • Cover the paint when you aren't using it.
Let each layer dry not checked yet

Let each layer dry

Not checked yet

  • Between steps, the paint underneath should be dry to the touch. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  • Painting into half-dry paint drags it up and turns it gooey and muddy.
  • Thick paint can feel dry on top and still be wet inside. Give thick areas longer.
  • Fine lines and light colors over dark especially need a dry layer underneath.
Light colors over dark need more than one coat not checked yet

Light colors over dark need more than one coat

Not checked yet

  • One coat of white or a light color over a dark one usually looks gray and patchy.
  • Expect two or three thin coats, letting each dry. Use the paint thick, with little water.
Making a color lighter or darker not checked yet

Making a color lighter or darker

Not checked yet

  • To lighten: add the color to the white a little at a time, not white to the color.
  • White also dulls a color. Too much turns it chalky.
  • To darken: add the dark into the lighter mix in small amounts.
  • For the next lighter value of something, start from the mix you already have and add white, so the colors stay related.
One light direction not checked yet

One light direction

Not checked yet

  • Pick where the light comes from and put every highlight on that side.
  • Each thing is built the same way: the whole shape in a darker or middle value, a lighter value on the side facing the light, then the lightest on a small area at the very edge. Each covers less than the one before.
The ugly stage not checked yet

The ugly stage

Not checked yet

  • Partway through, every painting looks flat or wrong. That's normal. Keep building.
  • Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.
  • Details come last, and only on shapes that are already right.
How much water not checked yet

How much water

Not checked yet

  • Keep water to about half the mix or less. More than that makes weak, see-through color that can lift when you paint over it.
  • For covering, use the paint thick, with little or no water.
  • After rinsing, wipe the metal part of the brush dry.

The misty sunset sky 4 steps

STEP 1 OF 18 · The misty sunset sky, 1 of 4

Cover the canvas with misty lavender-gray

  1. Inside the outlined area: the whole canvas.
  2. Paint: Misty lavender-gray.
  3. Mix enough Misty lavender-gray for this step and step 14; cover it between them.
  4. Brush: 1 inch flat. Load: An even coat, neither thick nor thin.
  5. Start with the darkest color and stroke side to side. Without rinsing, pick up the next lighter color and paint below it. Then stroke back up over the join several times.
  6. It should leave smooth bands of color, with a soft join where two wet colors meet.
  7. Watch out: A hard line where two colors meet. Fix: add more of the lighter color at the join and blend again.

Tip: The light comes from the low sun at the upper right, so every highlight in this lesson sits on that side and the cool gray stays at the left and bottom. Colors dry a little darker, so test each mix on the edge of your palette before a big area. Let the gray run right to all four edges.

Stroke: Side-to-side blend how to do it, not checked yet

Side-to-side blend

Not checked yet

With. wide flat; 3/4 inch wash brush

Load. An even coat, neither thick nor thin.

Motion. Start with the darkest color and stroke side to side. Without rinsing, pick up the next lighter color and paint below it. Then stroke back up over the join several times.

What it leaves. Smooth bands of color, with a soft join where two wet colors meet.

Then. Stroke back over each join while it's wet.

Blend two colors side to side

Dashed outline: what to paint in that picture. Arrows: which way to move the brush.

If it goes wrong.

  • A hard line where two colors meet. Add more of the lighter color at the join and blend again.
  • Two very different colors won't blend. Mix a bridge color from the two on the palette (pink and yellow make orange) and paint it between them.
  • The brush is overloaded. Wipe it on a rag. Rinse before going into white.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 2 OF 18 · The misty sunset sky, 2 of 4

Scrub in the dusty rose patches

  1. Let the misty sunset sky dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush fully first: this is the lightest paint yet.
  3. Inside the outlined area. It reaches all four edges of the canvas.
  4. Paint: Dusty rose-tan.
  5. Brush: 1 inch flat. Load: One or two colors on the brush. How much of each is on it controls the blend.
  6. Short strokes that cross each other in two directions, like overlapping X shapes.
  7. It should leave a soft, slightly textured blended fill with visible criss-cross marks.
  8. Leave what step 1 painted showing around these marks, as in the Result picture.

Tip: Scatter the patches loosely, mostly in the middle and toward the lower left, and leave plenty of the gray showing between them. Keep your crossing strokes short.

STEP 3 OF 18 · The misty sunset sky, 3 of 4

Glow gold around the sun

  1. Let the misty sunset sky dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush fully first: this is the lightest paint yet.
  3. Inside the outlined area. It reaches all four edges of the canvas.
  4. Paint: Sunset gold.
  5. Mix enough Sunset gold for this step and steps 7, 10 and 12; cover it between them.
  6. Brush: 3/4 inch flat.
  7. Make small circles with the tip of the brush, moving outward from the sun's spot, so the gold spreads in soft rings.
  8. It should leave soft rings of gold that fade out into the gray.
  9. Leave what steps 1 and 2 painted showing around these marks, as in the Result picture.
  10. Watch out: The glow has a hard edge. Fix: soften it with lighter passes of the same circles, fading outward.

Tip: Work outward from the upper right, where the sun will go, and let the gold fade out toward the left and bottom. Leave a round gap about 1 1/4 inches across for the sun itself.

Small circles

Motion. Small circles with the tip of the brush make a cloud's bumpy top edge. Around a sun or moon, circular strokes move outward from it.

What it leaves. A bumpy, soft edge.

Then. Smooth with the same circular motion, and highlight only the lit top edges.

Little circles along the top

Dashed outline: what to paint in that picture. Arrows: which way to move the brush.

If it goes wrong.

  • The edge is too hard. Soften it with lighter passes. On a cloud, smudging with a finger works too.

STEP 4 OF 18 · The misty sunset sky, 4 of 4

Dab in the sun

  1. Let the misty sunset sky dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush fully first: this is the lightest paint yet.
  3. Inside the outlined area. Its top is about 1 in from the top edge, and its right side is about 4 in from the right edge; it's about 1 1/4 in wide and 1 1/4 in tall.
  4. Paint: Sun cream.
  5. Brush: #8 round. Load: Little paint, fairly dry.
  6. Tap with the tip of the brush. The more you tap one spot, the more solid it gets.
  7. It should leave dots or dappled patches that get more solid the more you tap.
  8. Watch out: Blobs instead of dots. The brush is too wet or holds too much paint. Fix: wipe most of the paint off on a paper towel and tap again.
  9. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: Tap, don't stroke, so the sun is soft and glowing. Fill the round gap you left, and keep the edge a little fuzzy where it meets the gold.

Dabbing also called stippling

Not checked yet

Load. Little paint, fairly dry.

Motion. Tap with the tip of the brush. The more you tap one spot, the more solid it gets.

What it leaves. Dots or dappled patches that get more solid the more you tap.

Then. Tap a lighter mix on the lit side, leaving the darker taps showing underneath.

Tap, don't stroke

Dashed outline: what to paint in that picture. Arrows: which way to move the brush.

If it goes wrong.

  • Blobs instead of dots. The brush is too wet or holds too much paint. Wipe most of the paint off on a paper towel and tap again.
  • A patch went too solid. Tap over it with a lighter or darker mix to break it up.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

The far woods 3 steps

STEP 5 OF 18 · The far woods, 1 of 3

Pull down the far trunks

  1. Let the misty sunset sky dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush well first. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  3. Inside the outlined area, top to bottom to the right edge. Its left side is about 3 in from the right edge.
  4. Paint: Far trunk blue-gray.
  5. Brush: 3/4 inch flat. Load: Load the brush, then wipe it until only a little paint is left.
  6. Stroke straight down each trunk, starting at the top edge of the canvas, with light pressure.
  7. It should leave soft, streaky, see-through trunks that look misty and far away.

Tip: There are two main trunks near the right edge, and a few shorter ones lower down beside them. Wipe the brush nearly dry so they stay faint and far away. Run each one right off the top or bottom edge, and the foliage will cover their tops later.

Pull-down

With. #12 bright; flat

Load. Load the brush, then wipe it until only a little paint is left.

Motion. Stroke straight down, starting just below the thing being reflected.

What it leaves. A soft, streaky, see-through reflection of a tree, boat, or shore.

Then. Once dry, cross it with thin horizontal dashes of the water color.

Pull the color straight down

Dashed outline: what to paint in that picture. Arrows: which way to move the brush.

Don't be too exact. The water is moving, so a loose reflection looks right.

STEP 6 OF 18 · The far woods, 2 of 3

Dab the hazy orange foliage

  1. Let the far misty trunks and the misty sunset sky dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area. It reaches all four edges of the canvas.
  3. Paint: Hazy orange.
  4. Brush: 1/2 inch old stiff flat. Load: Little paint, fairly dry.
  5. Tap with the tip of the brush. The more you tap one spot, the more solid it gets.
  6. It should leave dots or dappled patches that get more solid the more you tap.
  7. Watch out: Blobs instead of dots. The brush is too wet or holds too much paint. Fix: wipe most of the paint off on a paper towel and tap again.

Tip: Make loose clumps, mostly on the left, the upper right around the sun, and the lower middle. Paint right over the gold glow where a clump goes, and leave the gray showing between the clumps. Don't worry about the bird's shape: the bird is painted on top later, so a little overlap is fine.

The branch 2 steps

STEP 8 OF 18 · The branch, 1 of 2

Paint the dark bark

  1. Let the far woods and the misty sunset sky dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush well first. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  3. Inside the outlined area. It reaches all four edges of the canvas.
  4. Paint: Bark brown.
  5. Brush: 1 inch flat.
  6. Bend every stroke along the branch, following its curve from the trunk out toward the twigs.
  7. It should leave marks that follow the curve of the branch, which is what makes it look round.

Tip: Start with the trunk on the left, then follow the thick curved limb to the right and thin the stroke out onto the twigs. Pull each stroke along the branch, not across it. Around now the painting looks messy: that's the ugly stage, and it's normal. Keep going.

STEP 9 OF 18 · The branch, 2 of 2

Dry brush the sunlit bark

  1. Let the branch and the far woods dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area, all the way across from the top edge. Its bottom is about 1/4 in from the bottom edge.
  3. Paint: Bark tan.
  4. Brush: 1/2 inch old stiff flat. Load: A dry brush, no water. Load only the tip, then wipe most of the paint off on a paper towel. It should feel dry and hard to apply.
  5. Light pressure, skimming the surface.
  6. It should leave feathery, broken, see-through marks that catch the canvas texture. Never a solid area.
  7. Leave what step 8 painted showing around these marks, as in the Result picture.
  8. Watch out: It went on solid. The brush was too loaded. Fix: let it dry, then dry-brush the base color back over part of it.
  9. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: The sun is at the upper right, so put the tan on the top and right-hand sides of the limb and leave the dark brown showing underneath and on the left side of the trunk.

The four leaves 2 steps

STEP 10 OF 18 · The four leaves, 1 of 2

Press in the golden leaves

  1. Let the branch and the far woods dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Optional: lightly chalk its outline first, from the transfer outline in Before you start, placed with the tape marks.
  3. Inside the outlined area, top to bottom. Its left side is about 1 in from the left edge and its right side is about 2 1/2 in from the right edge.
  4. Paint: Sunset gold.
  5. Brush: #8 round. Load: Paint loaded well into the belly of the brush, creamy, not runny.
  6. Touch down with the tip, press so the belly spreads, then pull and lift so the stroke ends on the tip.
  7. It should leave a teardrop or comma shape, wide where you pressed and pointed where you lifted.
  8. Watch out: A blob instead of a teardrop. Too much paint, or too slow a lift. Fix: use less paint and lift faster.

Tip: Two leaves hang at the upper left and two at the lower right, joined to the branch by thin stems. Press once for each lobe of the leaf, working from the stem out to the points. Gold is see-through, so paint it twice, letting the first coat dry.

Head, cheek and feet 3 steps

STEP 16 OF 18 · Head, cheek and feet, 1 of 3

Dab the black cap and bib

  1. Let the chickadee's body and the far woods dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area. Its top is about 1 1/4 in from the top edge, and its left side is about 5 in from the left edge; it's about 3 in wide and 2 1/2 in tall.
  3. Paint: Chickadee black.
  4. Brush: #6 round. Load: Little paint, fairly dry.
  5. Tap with the tip of the brush. The more you tap one spot, the more solid it gets.
  6. It should leave dots or dappled patches that get more solid the more you tap.
  7. Watch out: Blobs instead of dots. The brush is too wet or holds too much paint. Fix: wipe most of the paint off on a paper towel and tap again.

Tip: The cap covers the top of the head and the bib sits under the chin, with the white cheek left empty between them. Tap around the edge for a soft, fluffy outline. Leave a thin gap for the beak at the front, which is painted later.

STEP 17 OF 18 · Head, cheek and feet, 2 of 3

Press in the white cheek

  1. Let the black cap and bib, and the chickadee's body dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush well first. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  3. Inside the outlined area. Its top is about 2 1/2 in from the top edge, and its left side is about 5 1/2 in from the left edge; it's about 1 3/4 in wide and 3/4 in tall.
  4. Paint: Feather white.
  5. Brush: #4 round. Load: Paint loaded well into the belly of the brush, creamy, not runny.
  6. Touch down with the tip, press so the belly spreads, then pull and lift so the stroke ends on the tip.
  7. It should leave a teardrop or comma shape, wide where you pressed and pointed where you lifted.
  8. Feather white is much lighter than what it goes over: expect two or three thin coats, letting each dry.
  9. Watch out: A blob instead of a teardrop. Too much paint, or too slow a lift. Fix: use less paint and lift faster.

Tip: Paint the cheek in the gap between the black cap and the black bib, with the pointed end toward the beak. Feather white is much lighter than the black, so it needs two or three thin coats.

STEP 18 OF 18 · Head, cheek and feet, 3 of 3

Draw the legs and feet

  1. Let the chickadee's body and the branch dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush well first. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  3. Inside the outlined area. Its bottom is about 3 1/2 in from the bottom edge, and its left side is about 5 1/2 in from the left edge; it's about 2 1/2 in wide and 1 1/2 in tall.
  4. Paint: Slate gray.
  5. Brush: 10/0 liner. Load: Thin the paint with water until it flows like ink: swirl the brush in water, then in the paint. Reload often.
  6. Hold the brush upright, with light, steady pressure, and draw each thin leg in one flowing line. Let the toes wrap over the branch and wobble the edges a little.
  7. It should leave thin, flowing lines.
  8. Watch out: Skippy, broken lines. The paint is too thick. Fix: add water.
  9. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: Draw one thin leg from the belly down to each foot, then curl three short toes over the branch. When it's dry, use the same Slate gray to add the small beak at the front of the head, and dot the eye in last with the very tip of the brush. They're too small to be their own steps.

How Claude read your photosubject, light, layers

Before starting

Subject: a black-capped chickadee on an autumn branch (AI-made painting)

Found in the image: just the picture

Done: none

Why: no bars, borders or captions

Fitted to your canvas

Canvas: 11 x 14 in, landscape (14 x 11)

Done: crop

Left out: about 7.5% off each side: some empty haze on the left and the right-hand tree

Why: photo is 3:2, canvas 14:11, crop is free and keeps bird and branch whole

Beginner version

What made it too busy: no tiny separate things, foliage is soft big blobs, about 8 parts

Why: within detail_budget

A fat black-capped chickadee on a curved autumn branch, backlit by a low sun through hazy orange foliage and misty trunks. What matters: the bird's black cap and white cheek, the warm glow against cool lavender haze, and the branch's curve. Hard parts: soft blurry background (all haze), tiny feet, and the beak and eye.

Subject: A black-capped chickadee perched on an autumn branch
Focal point: the bird's head
Light: the low sun, upper right: warm light on the right of the bird and branch, cool blue-gray shadow on the left

What it saw, back to front

  1. Misty sunset sky
  2. The branch
  3. The four leaves
  4. The chickadee
  5. Legs and feet
Why this techniquePaint along, back to front

I chose it; the owner named no technique

ChosenPaint along, back to frontStart on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

Paint-along back to front is the owner's pick for beginner acrylic; the haze, foliage, branch, leaves, bird order is exactly back to front.

Passed onacrylic-block-in-beginner

decisions.md picked paint-along for acrylic beginners; block-in stays an option

How the paint recipes were worked out13 paints, free

Paint doesn't mix like light on a screen: blue and yellow make green, not gray. So the recipes come from a pigment mixing model (Mixbox), not a guess. For each paint it tried every simple recipe from your tubes, up to three colors plus white, and kept the one that lands closest to the color in the painting. Delta E is how far off it lands: under 2 is hard to see, under 5 is close, and over 8 means these tubes can't quite make it.

  • Misty lavender-gray Delta E 1.4
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 3 parts flesh tint, 1 part sky blue, 1 part ultramarine

  • Dusty rose-tan Delta E 1.2
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 3 parts white, 2 parts burnt umber, 1 part light olive green, a touch of purple red

  • Sun cream Delta E 0.7
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 3 parts white, 1 part medium yellow, a touch of purple red

  • Far trunk blue-gray Delta E 0.4
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 2 parts sky blue, 1 part burnt umber, a touch of cashew, a touch of white

  • Hazy orange Delta E 1.5
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 3 parts purple red, 2 parts medium yellow, 2 parts flesh tint, 1 part white

  • Sunset gold Delta E 0.7
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 3 parts medium yellow, 3 parts flesh tint, 1 part crimson

  • Bark brown Delta E 0.9
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 1 part burnt umber, a touch of purple red, a touch of light olive green

  • Bark tan Delta E 0.4
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 2 parts light olive green, 1 part purple red, a touch of crimson, a touch of white

  • Leaf red-orange Delta E 0.6
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 1 part medium yellow, 1 part crimson

  • Feather white Delta E 0.9
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 4 parts white, 1 part flesh tint, 1 part raw umber

  • Wing charcoal Delta E 2.7
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 2 parts raw umber, 1 part ultramarine, a touch of flesh tint, a touch of white

  • Chickadee black Delta E 1.2
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 2 parts raw umber, 1 part ultramarine

  • Slate gray Delta E 3.0
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 3 parts raw umber, 2 parts ultramarine, 1 part white

Furthest off: Delta E 3.0. Real tubes vary by brand, so mix, compare with the step picture, and nudge.

Why the steps go in this order18 steps

Sky and sun first, then far trunks and foliage over it (all behind), then the branch, then the leaves that hang from it, then the bird, with its body before wing, head, cheek and feet because each sits on the one before.

  1. 1. Cover the canvas with misty lavender-gray

    The farthest layer, covers the whole canvas first.

  2. 2. Scrub in the dusty rose patches

    Warm patches in the haze before the glow, so the gold sits on a warmed sky.

  3. 3. Glow gold around the sun

    Gold light around the sun, spreads from where the light comes from.

  4. 4. Dab in the sun

    The sun goes in its gap after the glow, brightest and last in the sky.

  5. 5. Pull down the far trunks

    Far trunks are behind the foliage, so they go before it.

  6. 6. Dab the hazy orange foliage

    Dark orange clumps give the foliage its base value.

  7. 7. Dab gold over the foliage

    Lighter gold over the orange, most near the sun.

  8. 8. Paint the dark bark

    The branch is in front of the woods, so it goes after them.

  9. 9. Dry brush the sunlit bark

    Sunlit tan over the dark bark, the second value.

  10. 10. Press in the golden leaves

    Leaves hang from the branch, so they go after it; all four start gold.

  11. 11. Press in the red leaves

    Two leaves turn red over the gold base.

  12. 12. Block in the round tan body

    The bird is the nearest thing, starting with its biggest shape.

  13. 13. Light the cream chest

    Cream light on the sun side over the tan body.

  14. 14. Paint the wing and tail gray

    Wing and tail lay in as one gray shape over the body.

  15. 15. Darken the wing feathers

    Dark feather stripes over the dry gray.

  16. 16. Dab the black cap and bib

    Black cap and bib once the body is dry.

  17. 17. Press in the white cheek

    The white cheek goes last in the head because it is lightest over black.

  18. 18. Draw the legs and feet

    Thin legs last, over the finished body and branch.

What the reviewer caught6 notes

A second Claude, with fresh eyes and none of this reasoning, compared each picture with its neighbors and the finish.
